Ephesians is written by a prisoner. Twice in these six chapters ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ calls himself a prisoner, and near the end he calls himself an ambassador in chains. Yet there is little in the letter about his own troubles. It is one of the most expansive things Paul ever wrote, a great sweep of praise and prayer about the purposes of God from before the creation of the world, and about the church that God is building out of Jews and Gentiles together.

⟦l:ephesus_400|Ephesus⟧ was one of the great cities of the Roman east, on the western coast of ⟦l:asia_108|Asia⟧ Minor, in what is now Turkey. It was the leading city of the province of Asia, a busy port and a centre of trade, with a vast theatre and a famous temple to the goddess Artemis, counted among the wonders of the ancient world. It was also known for magic and the practice of the occult.

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s history with ⟦l:ephesus_400|Ephesus⟧ is told in Acts. He first called there briefly at the end of his second journey, leaving his friends ⟦p:priscilla_2370|Priscilla⟧ and ⟦p:aquila_279|Aquila⟧ in the city. On his third journey he returned and stayed for about three years. He taught in the synagogue and then, when opposition grew, in a lecture hall belonging to a man named Tyrannus, and the message spread throughout the province. Many who had practised magic burned their books publicly. In the end the silversmiths, who made their living from shrines of Artemis, stirred up a riot in the theatre, and Paul left soon afterwards. On his last voyage to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ he called the elders of the Ephesian church to meet him at ⟦l:miletus_801|Miletus⟧, further down the coast, and said a tearful farewell, telling them they would not see him again.

What followed explains the chains. In ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ was seized in the temple courts, accused of bringing a Gentile into the area forbidden to non-Jews. Roman soldiers rescued him from the mob, and he was held for two years at ⟦l:caesarea_266|Caesarea⟧, on the coast, while Roman governors delayed his case. As a Roman citizen he appealed to the emperor, and he was sent to ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧, surviving a shipwreck on the way. Acts ends with him there under house arrest for two years, guarded by a soldier but free to receive visitors and to preach.

Ephesians is one of four letters ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ wrote from prison, along with Philippians, Colossians and the short letter to ⟦p:philemon_2342|Philemon⟧. They were written from ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧, in the early sixties of the first century. Ephesians and Colossians are closely related. They share many phrases and ideas, and both were carried by ⟦p:tychicus_2885|Tychicus⟧, a believer from the province of ⟦l:asia_108|Asia⟧ who had been among Paul's travelling companions at the end of his third journey.

The letter has an unusual character. Although ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ spent years in ⟦l:ephesus_400|Ephesus⟧, he sends no personal greetings, and at one point he speaks of having heard of his readers' faith. It reads less like news between friends than like a great unfolding of the gospel for every believer who would hear it read.

Most of its readers were Gentiles, who had once been, as ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ puts it, without hope and without God in the world. They lived in a city crowded with temples and shrines, and they were very aware of spiritual powers, which many people feared and tried to control through magic. Paul speaks to that world. Again and again he describes Christ raised far above every power and authority, and the church as the place where God is bringing together what was divided.

The letter falls into two halves. The first three chapters are almost entirely praise, prayer and explanation. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ blesses God for every spiritual blessing in Christ, describes how those who were dead in sin have been made alive by grace, and how the wall that divided Jew and Gentile has been broken down. Then, from chapter four, he turns to how his readers should live as a result: in unity, putting off their old way of life, within their households, and standing firm against spiritual opposition, clothed in the armour of God.
1:
After the briefest of greetings, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ begins with praise. In the original Greek, the passage that follows forms one long, unbroken sentence. It blesses God the Father for every spiritual blessing given to believers in Christ, and it traces those blessings from before the foundation of the world to the fullness of time, when God will bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ.

The passage moves through the work of the Father, who chose and adopted his people; the Son, in whom they have redemption and forgiveness; and the Holy Spirit, with whom they were sealed, the pledge of their inheritance. A refrain recurs three times: to the praise of his glory.

Then ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ turns from praise to prayer. He has heard of his readers' faith and love, and he prays that they will understand the hope of their calling and the greatness of God's power. That power, he says, is the same power God exercised when he raised Christ from the dead and seated him far above every ruler and authority, in this age and the age to come. In a city where people feared spiritual powers and sought protection through magic, that claim carried particular weight.
2:
⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ has just described the power of God that raised Christ from the dead and seated him far above every authority. Now he shows what that same power has done for his readers.

He begins with where they were. They were dead in their trespasses and sins, following the ways of the world and the ruler of the power of the air. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ includes himself and his fellow Jews too: all of us, he says, once lived this way. But God, rich in mercy, made them alive with Christ, raised them up and seated them with him in the heavenly realms. The middle of the chapter contains one of Paul's most compact statements of grace: it is by grace you have been saved, through faith, and this is not from yourselves.

The second half of the chapter turns to what divided Jews and Gentiles. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ reminds the Gentile believers that they were once excluded from Israel and strangers to God's covenants. In the temple in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, a stone barrier separated the court of the Gentiles from the inner courts, with notices warning foreigners not to go further, on pain of death. Paul speaks of Christ breaking down the dividing wall of hostility, making Jew and Gentile into one new man and building them together into a dwelling place for God.
3:
The last chapter ended with a new temple, built by God out of Jews and Gentiles together. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ now begins to pray for his readers, but almost immediately he breaks off. Having called himself the prisoner of Christ ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ for the sake of the Gentiles, he pauses to explain what that means.

He speaks of a mystery, in the sense ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ gives that word: something hidden in God for ages and now revealed. The mystery is that through the gospel the Gentiles are fellow heirs with Israel, members of the same body, sharing in the same promise. This, he says, is the message entrusted to him, less than the least of all the saints, to proclaim among the Gentiles. And through the church, God's wisdom is being displayed even to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms.

His imprisonment is part of this calling, and he asks his readers not to be discouraged by his sufferings. Then he resumes the prayer he began. He kneels before the Father and prays that they may be strengthened by ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧ and know the love of Christ in all its breadth, length, height and depth. The chapter, and the first half of the letter, ends in a hymn of praise.
4:
The first half of the letter closed with praise. Now ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ turns to how his readers should live, and he makes the connection plain: as a prisoner in the Lord, he urges them to walk in a manner worthy of their calling.

His first concern is unity. He has spent three chapters describing how God has made Jews and Gentiles into one body, and now he urges them to keep the unity of ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧. He lists what they share: one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all. Within that unity, Christ has given gifts to his people, and ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ quotes a psalm about a conqueror ascending on high and distributing gifts. Christ has given apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers to equip the church and help it grow to maturity.

The second half of the chapter turns to the change that faith in Christ brings. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ uses the picture of taking off old clothes and putting on new ones. The old self, with its former way of life among the Gentiles, is to be put off, and the new self put on. Then he gives a series of specific instructions about speech, anger, honest work and forgiveness.
5:
⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ continues his description of the new life. The last chapter ended with a call to forgive one another as God forgave them. Now he urges his readers to imitate God, as beloved children, and to walk in love, as Christ loved them and gave himself for them.

He then sets out the contrast between their former way of life and their new one. The religious and social life of a city like ⟦l:ephesus_400|Ephesus⟧ included festivals, banquets and drinking, sometimes with sexual licence attached. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ calls his readers to have nothing to do with such things, and uses the image of darkness and light. Once they were darkness; now they are light in the Lord. Instead of drunkenness, they are to be filled with ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧, singing psalms, hymns and spiritual songs.

The final part of the chapter begins a section on the household, a common topic in moral teaching of the ancient world. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ starts with husbands and wives. What he says about marriage leads him into a reflection on Christ and the church, using the words of Genesis about two becoming one flesh, which he calls a profound mystery.
6:
⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s instructions to the household continue from the last chapter. Having addressed wives and husbands, he now turns to children and fathers, and then to slaves and masters. In the Roman world a household could include several generations as well as slaves, and many of the earliest believers were slaves. Paul speaks to each group directly, and he grounds every instruction in their shared relationship to the Lord, who shows no favouritism.

Then he turns to his final appeal. Be strong in the Lord, he writes, and put on the full armour of God. The struggle believers face, he says, is not against flesh and blood, but against spiritual forces of evil. He describes the armour piece by piece: the belt, the breastplate, the shoes, the shield, the helmet and the sword. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ was writing as a prisoner, with Roman soldiers never far away, and much of his language comes from the prophet ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧.

The letter ends with a request for prayer, that ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ might speak boldly as an ambassador in chains. He commends ⟦p:tychicus_2885|Tychicus⟧, who is carrying the letter and will give them news of him, and closes with a blessing of peace and grace.
